newsitem.title: USA: Two Oklahoma bombing jurors excused from serving.
newsitem.headline: Two Oklahoma bombing jurors excused from serving.

text.p: A woman who disobeyed an order to avoid news and a retired federal government worker who did not know if he could be fair were dismissed on Friday from serving as jurors in the Oklahoma City bombing trial.

Federal Judge Richard Matsch's reaction was different in the two cases. He sympathised with the retired Federal Highway Administration employee but spoke sternly to the woman who read about a Justice Department study showing improprieties at the FBI crime lab.

"Given what you have said, I don't think there is any purpose in talking with you further. I am concerned you violated the court's rules and you'll hear from me about that," Matsch said as he dismissed the woman.
The judge, prosecutors and defence attorneys have questioned 91 candidates in 15 days to assemble a jury of 12 plus six alternates to decide the fate of Timothy McVeigh.
The Gulf War veteran has pleaded not guilty to the April 19, 1995, bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in Oklahoma City that killed 168. He faces the death penalty if convicted.

Security remained tight in Denver as the bombing anniversary approached. Concrete barricades circle the downtown Denver city block that houses the federal courthouse and mounted policemen were posted across the street from the courthouse.

The woman who read the news accounts -- the sixth person to be publicly dismissed -- knew about a Justice Department report issued this week that showed the FBI's crime laboratories provided flawed evidence in some major cases, including the Oklahoma City and World Trade Centre bombing cases.
Another woman who admitted in a previous session to paying attention to news reports had also incurred the judge's wrath.

The judge has not disclosed which potential jurors have been excused for specific reasons, such as total opposition to the death penalty. The jury panel is expected to be chosen by next week, with opening statements to follow.

Potential jurors are quizzed on a number of subjects, including their exposure to pre-trial publicity. While many say they inadvertently hear or read a snippet of a story, they also make valiant efforts to ignore bombing stories.
One man told the judge he sticks his fingers in his ears and hums so he will not hear anything on the Oklahoma bombing case.

The retired federal government worker was very emotional when he told the court: "I could have been in that building if I'd still been working. I'm pretty emotional about it," he said as his voice broke.
Matsch said in dismissing the man: "We appreciate your being very honest and we're going to excuse you in this case. It's too much to ask."
Another potential juror needed prompting from the judge before he remembered several run-ins with the law.

"It's coming back to you, is it?" Matsch asked the man who had failed to list on a 40-page questionnaire that he had paid a $50 fine after being charged with reckless endangerment. The man said he remembered the incident after the judge told him he had a computer printout of the record.

The man explained that he simply forgot the 1993 incident, in which his cat jumped on a kitchen table, knocking a .357 handgun to the floor, where it discharged a bullet that ricocheted off a television set and settled inside a wall.
